analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to vote to approve any major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 237-187 on January 5, 2017, but the Senate never voted on it, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The REINS Act would flip the default rule for major federal regulations. Today, a new rule takes effect unless Congress passes a resolution to reject it. Under this bill, any rule estimated to cost the economy $100 million a year or more would take effect only if both the House and Senate pass a joint resolution approving it and the president signs it — and if Congress does not act within 70 legislative days, the rule dies. The bill also requires agencies to repeal or amend other rules to fully offset the cost of any new rule, and over ten years it would require Congress to reapprove existing rules, with any rule Congress never approves ceasing to apply.
analysis.who_benefits: Large regulated companies and the industries that face costly new federal rules — on air and water pollution, workplace safety, product safety, consumer finance, and more. Under the bill, any new rule with an annual cost of $100 million or more would be presumptively dead unless both chambers of Congress affirmatively approved it, and agencies would have to offset new rule costs by repealing existing rules. Because Congress rarely passes a resolution for any individual rule — especially during divided government — most major rules would simply never take effect.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large regulated companies and trade groups

how_it_helps.text: Any 'major rule' — one the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs finds costs the economy $100 million a year or more, sharply raises prices, or significantly affects competition, employment, investment, or innovation — could not take effect unless Congress enacted a joint resolution of approval; if none passed within 70 legislative or session days, the rule would be deemed not approved and would not take effect.
Before any new rule could take effect, the issuing agency would have to amend or repeal other rules to completely offset the new rule's annual costs to the economy — a 'cut-go' requirement.

Beginning six months after enactment, agencies would have to submit each year at least 10% of their existing rules for congressional review, and ten years after enactment any existing rule Congress had not approved would no longer continue in effect.
Approval resolutions could not be amended at any stage, and the Senate would be required to vote within 15 session days after a committee reported or was discharged.
The bill exempted monetary policy rules from the Federal Reserve and rules governing hunting, fishing, and camping programs, which would take effect as agencies determine.

analysis.who_pays: People who rely on federal protections — clean air and water, workplace and food safety, drug and consumer-product safety, and consumer financial rules. Because Congress almost never passes a stand-alone resolution approving a specific regulation, most major rules would die by default, and the 90-day emergency exception covers only imminent health or safety threats, criminal-law enforcement, national security, and trade agreements. Federal agencies would also lose the ability to respond to new hazards with rules that actually take effect.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: The emergency carve-out is narrow: a major rule could take effect without congressional approval for only one 90-day period, and only if the president determines it is necessary because of an imminent threat to health or safety, to enforce criminal laws, for national security, or under a trade agreement — leaving most new protections to die if Congress does not act.

Existing protections would be put at risk over time: ten years after enactment, any rule in effect that Congress had not approved through the new procedure would no longer continue in effect, so long-standing rules could lapse if Congress simply failed to schedule votes on them.
Because approval resolutions cannot be amended, Congress could only vote yes or no on a rule as written — it could not fix a flawed rule without killing it.

Supporters' strongest argument in good faith: unelected agencies issue rules with multibillion-dollar costs that Congress never votes on, and requiring a recorded vote would make regulators accountable to voters and force Congress to write more detailed laws.

The 'cut-go' requirement sounds like fiscal discipline but operates as a one-way ratchet: an agency could not issue a new rule to address a new hazard without repealing other rules of equal cost, even when the new hazard is unrelated to the rules being repealed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument that Congress delegates too much lawmaking to agencies and that voters deserve recorded votes on costly rules. But the bill's design substitutes congressional inaction for agency judgment: in a body that struggles to pass budgets on time, most major rules — including protections for air, water, workplaces, food, and consumer finance — would die without ever getting a vote, and the cut-go requirement would force agencies to strip other protections to pay for new ones. The accountability benefit is speculative and generic; the cost would be specific rules that protect specific people, going unissued or lapsing. On balance, the trade heavily favors regulated industries.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it near party-line just two days into the new Congress, but it was referred to a Senate committee, got a hearing and never a floor vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House passed H.R. 26 on January 5, 2017, by a recorded vote of 237 to 187, with 235 of 240 Republicans voting yes and only 2 of 193 Democrats joining them.

Before final passage, House Democrats offered a motion to recommit — an instruction to add an amendment barring insurance issuers from eliminating, weakening, or reducing health coverage for dependents under 26 — which failed 190 to 235, with all 190 supporting votes coming from Democrats.
The Senate received the bill on January 6, 2017, and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; it was never brought to the Senate floor.
The Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship held a hearing on the bill on March 29, 2017, printing the hearing as S.Hrg. 115-21.
The bill received no further action and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the people who came out ahead were ordinary Americans who rely on federal health, safety, financial, and environmental rules, which kept their default protection: a new rule still takes effect unless Congress affirmatively rejects it. Regulated industries did not get the congressional-approval requirement or the cut-go offset mandate. Senate Republican leaders who never scheduled a vote retained the discretion to keep the measure off the floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyone relying on federal safety and consumer rules

for.name: Rep. Doug Collins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the REINS Act on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress.

for.name: 160 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican.

for.name: House Republican leadership
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor under a rule (H. Res. 22) within three days of the new Congress, limiting debate and structuring the amendment process.

against.name: Rep. Stephanie Murphy
against.what_they_did: Offered a motion to recommit instructing the bill to be amended to prohibit insurers from eliminating or reducing health coverage for dependents under 26; it failed 190-235.

against.name: House Democratic amendment sponsors
against.role: Members including Reps. Grijalva, Conyers, Nadler, Cicilline, Scott (VA), and McNerney
against.what_they_did: Offered floor amendments during House debate; the record shows most were rejected on voice votes later confirmed by recorded votes.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it passed the House.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split almost entirely by party: 235 of 240 Republicans voted yes versus 2 of 193 Democrats, and the Democratic motion to recommit on young-adult health coverage failed 190-235 along party lines.

industries.industry: Regulated industries broadly (energy, manufacturing, chemicals, financial and consumer-product firms)
industries.note: The bill makes any new major rule — one costing the economy $100 million a year or more — presumptively dead unless Congress passes and the president signs a resolution approving it, and it forces agencies to offset new rule costs by repealing other rules [S3][S4]. Industry's gain from fewer and slower rules is the public's loss of the protections those rules provide, and the ten-year review would even put existing rules at risk of lapsing [S3][S4].
